posts.headline: Answer the top questions before they ask
posts.x:
Write down the 5 questions you hear on every call: weekends? what towns? free estimates? financing? how soon?

Answer them on your website and in your Google profile description.
posts.long:
Every owner hears the same handful of questions on the phone:
- Do you work weekends?
- What towns do you cover?
- Do you charge for estimates?
- Do you offer financing?
- How soon can you come out?

Write short, honest answers and put them where people look before they call: an FAQ section on your website and your Google profile description.

People who already have their answers call ready to book. And search engines and AI assistants use those answers too.

posts.headline: Answer reviews within a day
posts.x:
A review answered the same day tells the next customer you pay attention.

Set one time each day, like after lunch, to check for new reviews and reply. Five minutes.
posts.long:
A review answered the same day tells the next customer something: this company pays attention.

A review answered three weeks later tells them something too.

Pick one time each day to check, like right after lunch. Reply to anything new. Most days it's under five minutes.

If a bad one comes in, take a breath first. Reply calm and short, and move the details offline.

posts.headline: Your truck is a billboard
posts.x: Your truck is seen by more people than any ad you'll buy. Keep it clean, put your website on it big enough to read at a red light, and park it facing the street.
posts.long:
Your truck gets seen by more people every week than most ads you'll ever buy.

Make it count:
- Keep it clean. A dirty truck says a lot about the work.
- Website big enough to read at a red light
- One clear line on what you do
- Park facing the street at jobs when it's safe

And make sure your techs drive like they're being watched. They are.

posts.headline: The neighbor note
posts.x:
After a job, drop a short note at the houses on each side: "We just finished work for your neighbor. If you ever need us, here's how to reach us."

No pitch. Just a friendly heads-up.
posts.long:
Neighbors see your truck in the driveway. They wonder what's going on and whether you're any good.

After a job, leave a short note at the houses on each side and across the street:

"We just finished some work for your neighbor. Sorry for any noise. If you ever need us, here's our info."

Keep the homeowner's details out of it. No pitch, no coupon. Just friendly and local. Neighbors trust what the house next door already chose.

posts.headline: Check Apple Maps and Bing too
posts.x:
Google isn't the only map. iPhone users search Apple Maps, and Bing powers a lot of other searches.

Claim your free listings on Apple Business Connect and Bing Places. Same name, address and hours as Google.
posts.long:
Google isn't the only map people use.

Every iPhone owner who asks Siri or taps Maps is searching Apple Maps. Bing powers searches in other places too, including some AI assistants.

Both are free to claim:
- Apple Business Connect
- Bing Places for Business (it can import your Google profile)

Use the exact same business name, address, phone and hours as your Google profile. Matching details everywhere helps people, and the search engines, trust you're real.

posts.headline: Holiday hours on Google
posts.x:
Closed for Thanksgiving or Christmas? Set special hours on your Google profile ahead of time.

Nothing loses a customer faster than showing up as open and not answering.
posts.long:
If you're closing or running short for a holiday, set special hours on your Google profile ahead of time.

When someone's heat is out on Christmas Eve, they'll check whether you're open. If Google says open and nobody answers, that's a lost call and often a bad review.

If you do run emergency calls on holidays, say that too. It's a selling point when everyone else is closed.

posts.headline: Ask for referrals when they thank you
posts.x:
The best time to ask for a referral is right after a customer says "thank you so much."

Try: "Glad we could help. If you know anyone who needs us, we'd love to help them too."
posts.long:
The best moment to ask for a referral is the second a customer says "Thank you so much."

They're happy, you're there, and it feels natural:

"I'm really glad we could help. Most of our work comes from people like you telling friends and family, so if anyone you know needs us, we'd love to help them too."

That's it. No card shoved in their hand, no pressure. Leave a couple of cards on the counter on your way out.

posts.headline: Follow up a quote with a quick video
posts.x:
A 30-second phone video beats another email: "Hey Mike, it's Dave. Just walking through the quote one more time, here's what's included."

People reply to faces.
posts.long:
Sending a quote follow-up? Try a 30-second phone video instead of another email.

"Hey Mike, it's Dave from the other day. Quick walk through what's in your quote, and why we recommended the bigger unit. Any questions, just reply."

It doesn't need to be polished. Holding the phone in your truck is fine.

People ignore emails. They watch a short video from someone they've met.

posts.headline: The 5-minute phone test
posts.x:
Pull up your own website on your phone. Can you call you in one tap? Book in two? See what towns you cover?

Most customers will only ever see your site on a phone.
posts.long:
Pull up your own website on your phone right now and time it.

- Can you find the phone number without scrolling?
- Does tapping it start a call?
- Can you request a visit in two taps?
- Is it clear what you do and where?
- Does it load in a few seconds on cell data?

Most of your customers will only ever see your website on a phone. If any answer is no, that's the first thing to fix.

posts.headline: When they ask the price on the phone
posts.x:
"How much is it?" is the most common question on the phone. Instead of dodging it, give an honest range and explain what changes it.

People hang up on dodgers.
posts.long:
"How much does it cost?" is the question you'll hear most on the phone.

Dodging it ("Well, we'd have to come out...") makes people hang up and call the next shop.

Try an honest range: "Most of these run between X and Y. Where it lands depends on what we find, like how old the system is. The visit lets us give you an exact number."

Now they know you're not hiding anything, and the visit sounds useful, not like a trap.

posts.headline: Ask what you did, not for keywords
posts.x:
Want reviews that mention your service and town? Don't script them. Ask, "What was the biggest difference after we finished?"

People describe it in their own words, and that's what reads real.
posts.long:
A lot of owners want reviews that mention the service and the town. Handing customers a script makes reviews read fake.

Instead, ask a good question when you request the review:

"Would you mind sharing what the biggest difference was after we finished?"

People naturally say things like "the house finally stays warm upstairs" or "they fixed our leak in Smyrna same day." Real words, real details. That's what convinces the next customer.

posts.headline: Build a seasonal reminder calendar
posts.x:
Write down what every past customer will need and when: spring tune-ups, fall checks, filter changes, gutter cleaning.

Then send the reminder before they think of it.
posts.long:
Most of what you do comes around on a schedule: spring AC checks, fall furnace tune-ups, water heater flushes, dryer vent cleaning, gutter cleanouts.

Build a simple calendar: what each past customer is likely to need, and when.

Then reach out a few weeks before they'd think of it themselves. "It's about time for your fall check. Want me to get you on the list before it gets busy?"

The company that reminds them is usually the one that gets the job.

posts.headline: Book the next visit before you leave
posts.x:
Before you pack up, ask: "Want me to put you down for your next check now? We'll remind you the week before."

Easiest booking you'll ever get.
posts.long:
Before you pack up the truck, ask one more question:

"Want me to go ahead and put you down for your next check in the spring? We'll send a reminder the week before."

They're already happy with you. They trust you. Saying yes takes two seconds.

It's the easiest booking you'll ever get, and it keeps them from calling someone else later.

posts.headline: Fill in every service on your Google profile
posts.x:
Your Google profile has a Services section. List every job you do, with a sentence on each.

Google uses it to match you to searches. If it's empty, you're invisible for those jobs.
posts.long:
Your Google Business Profile has a Services section, and a lot of companies leave it nearly empty.

List every job you do, not just the main ones. Add a plain one or two sentence description for each.

"Water heater replacement. Same-week installs for tank and tankless water heaters, old unit hauled away."

Google uses this to match you to what people search. If a service isn't listed, it's harder for you to show up for it.

posts.headline: Mention financing early
posts.x:
If you offer financing, say so on your website, your quotes and your Google profile.

A lot of people don't call because they assume they can't afford it.
posts.long:
If you offer financing, don't save it for the end of the sales talk.

Put it where people look before they call:
- Your website, near the top
- Your Google profile and services
- Every quote you send

A lot of homeowners never call because they assume a big repair is out of reach. Knowing there's a monthly option up front gets them to pick up the phone.

posts.headline: Register their warranty for them
posts.x: Registering the equipment warranty for the customer is a small thing that builds big trust. Then send them a note when it's done.
posts.long:
When you install new equipment, register the manufacturer warranty for the customer, then send a short note:

"All set, your warranty is registered. Here's the confirmation for your records."

It's ten minutes for you. For them it's one less thing to deal with and proof you looked out for them.

It's also a natural reason to be back in touch, and to ask how everything's running.

posts.headline: Same name, number and address everywhere
posts.x:
Check your business name, phone and address on Google, Facebook, Yelp, your website and your truck. They should match exactly.

Mismatches confuse customers and search engines.
posts.long:
Look up your business on Google, Facebook, Yelp, Nextdoor, Apple Maps and your own website.

Are the name, phone number and address exactly the same everywhere?

Old phone numbers, "LLC" on some and not others, a past address. It happens to most companies over the years.

Mismatches confuse customers, and search engines trust a business more when its details line up. Fix them one at a time.

posts.headline: Help in local groups without selling
posts.x:
When someone in a local Facebook group asks "Is this normal?" about their furnace or a leak, answer the question. Don't pitch.

Helpful answers get remembered.
posts.long:
Local Facebook groups and Nextdoor are full of people asking, "Is this normal?" about a noise, a leak, a breaker that keeps tripping.

Answer the question. Clearly and honestly, even if the answer is "That's an easy fix, here's what to check."

Don't drop your number or a sales pitch. Your name and company are on your profile.

The owner who keeps giving good free answers is the one people tag when someone needs a pro.

posts.headline: Your email signature works for you
posts.x:
Every email you send can carry your website, your service area and a link to your reviews.

Two minutes to set up. Seen hundreds of times a month.
posts.long:
Every email you and your office send is a chance to show people where to find you.

A good signature has:
- Your name and title
- Company name
- Website
- The towns you serve
- A link to your Google reviews

Two minutes to set up. Then it's seen on every email, every month, for free.

posts.headline: Keep a lost-quote log
posts.x:
When a quote doesn't close, write down why, if you know: price, timing, went with someone else, never answered.

After 20, you'll see a pattern you can fix.
posts.long:
Every time a quote doesn't turn into a job, jot down why, if you know:
- Price
- Timing
- Chose another company
- Decided to wait
- Never heard back

It only takes a few seconds a quote.

After 20 or 30, a pattern shows up. Maybe most "never heard back" quotes went out late. Maybe you're losing on one type of job. Now you know exactly what to fix.

posts.headline: Running late? Text early
posts.x:
If the tech is going to be late, text the customer as soon as you know, not when you're already late.

People forgive late. They don't forgive being left waiting with no word.
posts.long:
Jobs run long. Traffic happens. Being late is sometimes out of your hands.

What isn't: when you tell them.

Text the customer the moment you know you're running behind, not ten minutes after the window closed:

"Hi Karen, it's Josh. My last job is running long, I'll be there closer to 2:30. Sorry about that."

People forgive late. They don't forgive waiting by the window with no word.

posts.headline: Leave a sticker on the equipment
posts.x:
Put a small sticker with your name and website on the unit, panel or water heater you worked on.

When it needs service, they won't have to search.
posts.long:
After you service a unit, a water heater or a panel, leave a small sticker with your company name and website on it.

Years later, when something goes wrong, they'll walk over to it, see your name, and look you up.

No searching, no comparing five companies. It's one of the cheapest things you'll ever buy, and one of the hardest working.

posts.headline: Ask happy customers for photos
posts.x:
A homeowner's own photo of your work, with their OK, is better proof than any stock image.

When they send a thank-you, ask if you can share it.
posts.long:
Sometimes a happy customer texts you a photo: the finished bathroom, the new deck, the kids warm by the vent.

Ask if you can share it on your Google profile or social pages. Keep their name and address out unless they say otherwise.

Real photos from real customers are more convincing than anything you could stage. And most people are flattered to be asked.

posts.headline: Keep every past customer in one list
posts.x:
Your past customers are scattered across invoices, texts and old notebooks. Put them in one simple list: name, contact, what you did, when.

It's the most valuable list you own.
posts.long:
Most companies have their past customers scattered everywhere: old invoices, phone contacts, texts, a notebook in the truck.

Pull them into one simple list:
- Name
- How to reach them
- What you did
- When you did it

A spreadsheet is fine. Once it's in one place, you can send seasonal reminders, ask for reviews, and reach out in slow months.

You already paid to earn those customers. Don't lose them.

posts.headline: Get ready for busy season in the slow season
posts.x: Slow season is when you fix the things you won't have time for in July: update your Google profile, clean up the website, train the new guy, restock the trucks.
posts.long:
When the phone is quiet, it's tempting to just wait it out.

Slow season is the best time to fix what you won't have time for when it's busy:
- Update your Google profile photos and services
- Fix the website issues you keep meaning to get to
- Train new techs on how to greet customers
- Restock and organize the trucks
- Reach out to past customers

The work you do in the slow months shows up in the busy ones.

posts.headline: Claim your Nextdoor business page
posts.x:
A lot of neighbors ask Nextdoor for recommendations before they ask Google.

Claim your free business page so recommendations land on you.
posts.long:
A lot of homeowners ask their neighbors before they ask Google. On Nextdoor, "Who do you use for...?" is one of the most common posts.

Claim your free Nextdoor business page. When a neighbor recommends you, it links straight to your page, and the recommendations stack up over time.

Ask a few happy customers who use Nextdoor to recommend you there. Local word of mouth, written down.

posts.headline: How your techs say hello
posts.x:
The first 30 seconds at the door set the tone: name, company, a handshake if they want one, and "Where would you like me to start?"

Train it like any other skill.
posts.long:
The first 30 seconds at the front door shape the whole visit.

A simple greeting your techs can use every time:
- Smile, name and company: "Hi, I'm Marcus with Smith Plumbing."
- Confirm why they're there
- Ask, "Where would you like me to start?"
- Mention shoe covers before they ask

Most customers decide how they feel about your company before the tool bag is open. Train the greeting like any other skill.

posts.headline: Reply to every message on your profiles
posts.x:
Messages on your Google profile and Facebook page count as leads. Answer them as fast as a phone call.

An unanswered message is a lead you paid for and lost.
posts.long:
People message businesses through Google, Facebook and Instagram more than ever, especially after hours.

Treat those messages like phone calls. Turn on notifications, and make sure someone owns them.

Even a quick "Got your message! We'll call you first thing tomorrow" keeps the lead warm.

An unanswered message isn't just slow service. It's a customer who reached out and heard nothing.

posts.headline: Write the job notes for the next tech
posts.x:
Good job notes save the next visit: model numbers, where the shutoff is, the dog's name, what you recommended.

The customer notices when the next tech already knows.
posts.long:
After every job, leave good notes in the customer's file:
- Equipment make, model and age
- Where the shutoffs and access are
- What you recommended but they didn't do yet
- Little things: the dog's name, park on the street

When the next tech shows up already knowing all that, the customer notices. It feels like you remember them, because you do.

posts.headline: Say thank you in the slow months
posts.x:
Send past customers a simple thank-you in a slow month. No offer, no sales pitch. Just thanks.

They'll remember who stayed in touch.
posts.long:
In a slow month, send your past customers a short thank-you. No coupon, no offer.

"Just wanted to say thanks for trusting us this year. We really appreciate it."

It feels almost too simple. But most companies only reach out when they want something, so a plain thank-you stands out.

When they need help again, they'll think of the company that stayed in touch for no reason.
